subtitle: The reactive client store for your API

chapters.title: The Reactive Client Store
chapters.blurb: How collections, live queries, and optimistic mutations fit together into one fast client store.

steps.title: The Reactive Client Store
steps.coverSubtitle: Collections, live queries, and optimistic writes
steps.spoken: Tanstack DB is a reactive client store that sits between your components and your API, and makes interactions feel instant.
steps.displayNarration: **TanStack DB** is *the reactive client store for your API* — it extends TanStack Query with **collections**, **live queries**, and **optimistic mutations**.

steps.title: Two evils, one new way
steps.spoken: Most apps choose between view-specific endpoints that complicate the backend, or loading everything and filtering, which feels sluggish. Tanstack DB offers a third way: load normalized data into collections on the client.
steps.displayNarration: Instead of *view-specific APIs* (endpoint sprawl) or *load-everything-and-filter* (slow), TanStack DB loads data into **normalized collections** — created with `createCollection`.

steps.title: Data loads into the collection
steps.spoken: A collection is a typed set of objects, populated from your API. That can be a REST endpoint or a real-time sync engine, but your component never has to care which.
steps.displayNarration: A **collection** is a typed set of objects populated from **your API** — a REST endpoint via TanStack Query, or a sync engine. The component is decoupled from the source.

steps.title: Components read with live queries
steps.spoken: Your component reads the data with a live query. It is reactive: when the underlying rows change, only the affected results recompute, usually in well under a millisecond, and the component re-renders.
steps.displayNarration: Your component binds data with `useLiveQuery` — a **live query** that updates *incrementally* and sub-millisecond when collection rows change.

steps.title: Writes apply optimistically
steps.spoken: When the user acts, the component writes straight to the collection. The change shows up instantly, taking the network off the interaction path.
steps.displayNarration: On interaction the component calls `collection.update(id, draft => …)`. The write applies **optimistically** and instantly — the network is off the interaction path.

steps.title: Then it persists in the background
steps.spoken: Behind the scenes, the collection's handler writes the change to your API and the updated server state syncs back. Your backend stays simple.
steps.displayNarration: In the background the collection's handler persists to **your API**, then the server state syncs back. *Your backend stays simple.*

steps.title: Three pillars, one store
steps.spoken: Collections to load data, live queries to read it fast, and optimistic mutations to write it instantly. That is the whole development model, and the rest is detail.
steps.displayNarration: **Collections** load · **live queries** read · **optimistic mutations** write. Three pillars of TanStack DB's development model.

chapters.title: Defining Collections
chapters.blurb: Where collection data comes from — REST via TanStack Query, or a sync engine — and how the sync interface fills it.

steps.title: Defining Collections
steps.coverSubtitle: REST, sync engines, and the sync interface
steps.spoken: A collection is only as good as where it gets its data. This is how you point one at your backend, and how you'd host it in production.
steps.displayNarration: **Collections** decouple *loading* data from *binding* it to components. You choose a **collection options creator** for your data source.

steps.title: createCollection takes options
steps.spoken: Every collection is built by passing an options object to createCollection. The options decide where data comes from and how writes go back out.
steps.displayNarration: `createCollection(options)` builds a **collection**. The *options creator* you pass determines the data source and the mutation handlers.

steps.title: Option 1 — your REST API
steps.spoken: For an existing REST API, use query collection options. It fetches with Tanstack Query, so your current endpoints become the source, and you host nothing new.
steps.displayNarration: `queryCollectionOptions({ queryKey, queryFn })` loads from **your REST API** via TanStack Query. Keep the backend you already run in production.

steps.title: Option 2 — a sync engine
steps.spoken: For real-time, point electric collection options at a sync engine like Electric S Q L. It streams filtered shapes out of Postgres, and you can self-host it. PowerSync and TrailBase work the same way.
steps.displayNarration: `electricCollectionOptions({ shapeOptions })` syncs **shapes** out of Postgres via ElectricSQL. Self-hostable; *PowerSync* and *TrailBase* fit the same slot.

steps.title: Both speak one sync interface
steps.spoken: Whichever source you pick, it drives the same small sync interface. It begins a batch, writes each changed row, then commits, exactly like a database transaction.
steps.displayNarration: Every options creator drives the same `SyncConfig`: `begin()`, `write(message)`, `commit()`. A uniform funnel for any data source.

steps.title: Rows land, collection turns ready
steps.spoken: Written rows settle into the synced data, the immutable base every read sees. Once the first batch is in, the source calls mark ready and queries can run.
steps.displayNarration: Committed rows fill `syncedData` — the *immutable base*. `markReady()` flips the collection from loading to **ready**.

steps.title: Load eagerly or on demand
steps.spoken: You also choose how much to load. Eager mode pulls the whole collection up front; on-demand mode loads only what queries ask for, so your component's query becomes the request.
steps.displayNarration: Sync modes tune loading: **eager** (default, small sets), **on-demand** (large datasets — the query becomes the API call), **progressive** (instant subset, full set in background).

steps.title: Pick a source, get a collection
steps.spoken: REST through query options, or real-time through a sync engine, both flow through the same interface into a ready collection. That is how you wire Tanstack DB to production data.
steps.displayNarration: Source → options creator → `SyncConfig` → `syncedData` → **ready collection**. The same pipeline whether you host a REST API or a sync engine.

chapters.title: Live Queries
chapters.blurb: How declarative queries compile to an IR and run on differential dataflow for sub-millisecond incremental updates.

steps.title: Live Queries
steps.spoken: Live queries are what make reads feel instant. Let's see how a query you write turns into incremental updates.
steps.displayNarration: **Live queries** read data out of collections and update *incrementally* — built on **differential dataflow** for sub-millisecond results.

steps.title: You declare what you want
steps.spoken: You write a query the way your component needs the data: from a collection, filtered with where, maybe joined and projected with select. It reads like a typed query builder.
steps.displayNarration: `useLiveQuery(q => q.from({ todo }).where(…).select(…))` — a typed `queryBuilder` chain of `from`, `where`, `join`, `select`.

steps.title: It compiles to a QueryIR
steps.spoken: The builder doesn't run your functions directly. It compiles them into an intermediate representation, a plain object describing the query as references and expressions.
steps.displayNarration: The chain compiles to a `QueryIR`: a `from`, `where`, `join`, `select` tree of `CollectionRef`, `PropRef`, and `BasicExpression` nodes.

steps.title: The IR becomes a dataflow graph
steps.spoken: That representation is compiled into a differential dataflow pipeline using d2 t s. The source collections feed their rows into the graph as a stream of changes.
steps.displayNarration: The `QueryIR` compiles to a **d2ts** differential-dataflow graph. **Source collections** feed rows in as a change stream, not a snapshot.

steps.title: Out comes a result collection
steps.spoken: The graph produces a result, and that result is itself a collection. Your component binds to it and renders the rows.
steps.displayNarration: The graph emits a **result collection** — itself queryable. `useLiveQuery` returns its rows and re-renders the component.

steps.title: One change, recomputed in microseconds
steps.spoken: Now the magic: when a single row changes, the graph updates only what that change touches, instead of re-running the whole query. Updating one row in a hundred thousand takes under a millisecond.
steps.displayNarration: On a change, differential dataflow recomputes *only the affected output* — ~0.7ms to update one row in a 100,000-item sorted collection.

steps.title: Joins across collections
steps.spoken: Because every query reads collections and returns a collection, you can join across them, denormalizing synced data and even mixing in data from another source, all in the client.
steps.displayNarration: Live queries `join` across collections — denormalize synced data, or unify a database table with an external API, entirely client-side.

steps.title: Declare, compile, react
steps.spoken: You declare the query, it compiles to an intermediate representation, runs as differential dataflow, and re-renders incrementally. That is why complex reads stay sub-millisecond.
steps.displayNarration: `useLiveQuery` → `QueryIR` → **d2ts** dataflow → **result collection** → re-render. Declarative in, incremental out.

chapters.title: Optimistic Mutations
chapters.blurb: How a local write applies instantly as optimistic state, persists through a handler, and rolls back on failure.

steps.title: Optimistic Mutations
steps.spoken: Writes are where Tanstack DB feels magical. Let's follow one update from click to confirmed.
steps.displayNarration: Collections support `insert`, `update`, and `delete`. Each applies **optimistically** first, then persists. This is the *instant inner loop*.

steps.title: A local write
steps.spoken: The user completes a todo, so the component calls update on the collection with a draft. No await, no spinner, no request on the interaction path.
steps.displayNarration: `todoCollection.update(id, draft => { draft.completed = true })` — a synchronous local write. No `await` on the click.

steps.title: Optimistic state, layered on
steps.spoken: The collection keeps optimistic changes separate from the synced data. Your write goes into an overlay that sits on top of the immutable base, so reads see it immediately.
steps.displayNarration: The collection holds optimistic state *separately* from `syncedData`. The write lands in `optimisticUpserts`, overlaid on the immutable base — visible instantly.

steps.title: Wrapped in a transaction
steps.spoken: Under the hood the mutation becomes a transaction. It starts pending, holding the optimistic state, then moves to persisting once it begins talking to your server.
steps.displayNarration: The mutation is wrapped in a `Transaction` (`createTransaction`). It starts **pending** — holding optimistic state — then transitions to **persisting**.

steps.title: The handler persists it
steps.spoken: Persisting runs the collection's handler for this kind of write. The on-update handler reads the mutation and sends it to your backend, the only place network actually happens.
steps.displayNarration: Persisting invokes the collection's `onUpdate` handler. It reads `transaction.mutations[0]` and writes to **your backend** — the one place the network is touched.

steps.title: Confirmed, then dropped
steps.spoken: When the handler resolves, the server change syncs back into the synced data. The optimistic overlay is no longer needed, so it's dropped, and the two views agree.
steps.displayNarration: When the handler resolves, the write **syncs back** into `syncedData` and the optimistic overlay is discarded — synced and local views converge.
sourceRefs: docs/overview.md: held until the handler resolves

steps.title: On failure, roll back
steps.spoken: If the handler throws, the transaction rolls back. The optimistic overlay is removed and the user instantly sees the true server state again. No half-applied writes.
steps.displayNarration: If the handler *throws*, `tx.rollback()` removes the optimistic overlay and the UI snaps back to synced state. No partial writes survive.
sourceRefs: docs/overview.md: optimistic state is rolled back

steps.title: Instant now, durable soon
steps.spoken: Write locally, see it instantly, persist in the background, and either confirm or roll back. For richer flows, create optimistic actions or whole transactions by hand.
steps.displayNarration: `update` → optimistic overlay → `Transaction` → handler → backend → confirm or `rollback`. Use `createOptimisticAction` / `createTransaction` for custom flows.

chapters.title: Uni-directional Data Flow
chapters.blurb: The whole loop end to end — and how to back collections in production with your API or a sync engine.

steps.title: Uni-directional Data Flow
steps.coverSubtitle: Two loops, one direction — and going to production
steps.spoken: Put it all together and Tanstack DB extends redux-style one-way data flow past the client, all the way to your server.
steps.displayNarration: TanStack DB models **uni-directional data flow** — a fast *inner loop* of optimistic state, superseded by a slower *outer loop* of server persistence and sync.

steps.title: The read path
steps.spoken: Your component reads through a live query over the collection. Data flows out of the collection, into the query, and onto the screen.
steps.displayNarration: Reads flow one way: **collection** → **live query** → **component**. The local view drives the UI.

steps.title: The inner loop is instant
steps.spoken: A write goes the same one direction: into the collection as optimistic state, which immediately flows back out through the live query. The user sees the change at once.
steps.displayNarration: A write enters the **collection** optimistically and flows straight back out via the live query — the *inner loop* completes with no network.
sourceRefs: docs/overview.md: instant inner loop of optimistic state

steps.title: The outer loop persists
steps.spoken: Then the slower outer loop runs. The mutation handler persists the change to your A P I, which commits it to your database.
steps.displayNarration: The *outer loop*: the collection hands the mutation to your **handler**, which persists to **your API** and database.
sourceRefs: docs/overview.md: slower outer loop of persisting

steps.title: Server state syncs back
steps.spoken: The committed change streams back into the same collection. With a sync engine like Electric, the write returns a transaction id, and the collection waits to see that id arrive before dropping its optimistic copy.
steps.displayNarration: The server change **streams back** into the collection. Electric returns a `txid`; the collection matches it on the sync stream before clearing optimistic state.
sourceRefs: docs/overview.md: synced the updated server state back

steps.title: Hosting it in production
steps.spoken: So to run this in production you host two things you already understand: your own A P I for writes, and a source for reads. That source is either the same REST API, or a sync engine like Electric S Q L, PowerSync, or TrailBase, each self-hostable next to your Postgres.
steps.displayNarration: **In production:** keep your own API for writes; back reads with that same REST API (`queryCollectionOptions`) or a sync engine — ElectricSQL, PowerSync, TrailBase — self-hosted beside Postgres.

steps.title: One todo, all the way around
steps.spoken: Click to optimistic state, optimistic state to your A P I, your A P I to the sync stream, and the stream back into the collection where the live query renders it. One todo, one direction, the whole loop.
steps.displayNarration: The full circuit: **write** → **handler** → **API** → **sync stream** → **collection** → **live query** → **component**. Uni-directional, end to end.
